# AI Coding Tools: How to Choose the Right One for Your Project

Choosing an AI coding tool is really choosing a teammate with a specific working style: inline autocomplete, repo-wide chat, or full multi-file edits. The decision depends on your stack, your privacy needs, and whether you want help in the editor or a separate agent. Match the tool to how your team already works

## The tools worth considering

The following tools cover different parts of the job. Every section states the job, the strengths and the honest limits — enough to decide whether it fits without a trial

## GitHub Copilot

GitHub Copilot is a widely used AI coding assistant that suggests code directly inside VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, Neovim, and other editors

For coding, it helps with inline suggestions: Accept or edit completions as you write code

What GitHub Copilot is good at:
- Works across many popular editors and programming languages
- Context-aware completions fit the surrounding code style closely

Where GitHub Copilot is honest about limits:
- Requires a paid subscription for most individual users
- Signing in can require a VPN in some regions

Best for professionals users: [[link:/tools/7|GitHub Copilot]]

## Cursor

Cursor is an AI-first code editor built around pair programming with a model

For coding, it helps with repo-wide chat: Ask questions about code across the whole project

What Cursor is good at:
- AI features built into the editor, not bolted on
- Repository-wide context improves relevance of code suggestions

Where Cursor is honest about limits:
- Requires a paid plan for heavy AI usage
- Needs a VPN in some regions to sign in

Best for professionals users: [[link:/tools/13|Cursor]]

## Codeium

Codeium Codeium was Exafunction's free AI coding toolkit with inline completions and code search across many editors

For coding, it helps with inline completions: Autocomplete code inside VS Code and JetBrains editors

What Cursor is good at:
- Free tier covered individual developers without a paid plan
- Lightweight extension fits into existing editor workflows easily

Where Cursor is honest about limits:
- Repeated rebrands and ownership changes make the roadmap unclear
- Users must decide between Windsurf plugins and Devin Desktop

The learning curve fits free users, which is what [[link:/tools/1565|Codeium]] is aimed at

## Tabnine

Tabnine is an AI coding assistant offering code completion and chat inside popular IDEs

For coding, it helps with local completion: Run code completion fully on your own machine or servers

What Tabnine is good at:
- Can run fully locally or self-hosted on company servers
- Team-level policy controls limit what code the model sees

Where Tabnine is honest about limits:
- Access may require a VPN in some regions
- Running locally requires more local compute than cloud-based assistants

The learning curve fits developers users, which is what [[link:/tools/17|Tabnine]] is aimed at

## Replit AI

Replit AI An AI pair programmer inside Replit's cloud IDE that scaffolds apps, explains code and deploys them without local setup

For coding, it helps with quick prototyping: Start a project in the browser without installing anything locally

What Replit AI is good at:
- No local setup; coding, explaining, and deploying happen in the browser
- Fits beginners and teams who want a shared cloud environment

Where Replit AI is honest about limits:
- Requires a reliable internet connection and a browser to work
- Access needs a VPN in some regions, and the free plan is limited

Best for developers users: [[link:/tools/85|Replit AI]]

## Codium AI

Codium AI Now known as [[link:/tools/1454|Qodo]], this tool focuses on code quality rather than speed

For coding, it helps with unit test generation: Create behavior-focused unit tests for existing code functions

What Qodo is good at:
- Focuses on test coverage and correctness, not autocomplete
- Runs both in the IDE and in CI pipelines

Where Qodo is honest about limits:
- Requires setup time to tune rules and thresholds

The learning curve fits developers users, which is what [[link:/tools/83|Codium AI]] is aimed at

## CodeWhisperer

CodeWhisperer is Amazon's AI code assistant, built as a plugin for VS Code and JetBrains

For coding, it helps with aws development: Suggest SDK calls and service patterns for cloud apps

What CodeWhisperer is good at:
- Deep integration with AWS services and SDK examples
- Reference tracker shows whether suggestions resemble open-source code

Where CodeWhisperer is honest about limits:
- Suggestions are strongest when working inside AWS projects
- Outside AWS, offers less advantage than general assistants

The learning curve fits aws users, which is what [[link:/tools/233|CodeWhisperer]] is aimed at

## CodeGeeX

CodeGeeX is an open-source AI code model developed at Tsinghua University for multilingual programming

For coding, it helps with code completion: Inline multilingual suggestions while writing in your IDE

What CodeGeeX is good at:
- Open-source weights allow self-hosting and customization for research
- Handles multiple programming languages in a single assistant

Where CodeGeeX is honest about limits:
- May lag behind commercial models on complex refactoring tasks
- Documentation and plugin setup can be less polished

[[link:/tools/237|CodeGeeX]] is aimed at open source

## Kite

[[link:/tools/355|Kite AI]]-powered code completions for Python and JavaScript

For coding, it helps with python autocomplete: Get line and function completions while writing Python in supported editors

What Kite AI is good at:
- Completely free to use, with no subscription or usage limits
- Completions run locally, so code never leaves your machine

Where Kite AI is honest about limits:
- The project has been discontinued and receives no updates or support
- Language coverage is limited to Python and JavaScript only

[[link:/tools/474|Kite]] suits python users best

## How to choose

- Want suggestions as you type? GitHub Copilot, Codeium, or Tabnine.
- Want to chat across the whole repo? Cursor or [[link:/tools/477|Cody]].
- Privacy or air-gapped? Tabnine, Cody, or [[link:/tools/482|Continue.dev]] run locally.
- Language matters. Kite and CodeGeeX cover specific ecosystems.
- Try a free tier first; editor fit is personal and hard to predict

## A chaining workflow that works

Autocomplete in the editor with [[link:/tools/1565|Codeium]], refactor across files with [[link:/tools/13|Cursor]], and review changes with [[link:/tools/83|Codium AI]] before merging. Continue.dev keeps it all offline if privacy demands

## Common mistakes

- Picking the most famous tool without testing editor fit.
- Letting the assistant write code you don't understand—review everything.
- Ignoring privacy. Cloud tools send context off your machine.
- Skipping the security review on generated code

## FAQ

### GitHub Copilot or Cursor?

Copilot suggests inline as you type; Cursor offers repo-wide chat and multi-file edits. Pick by whether you want a suggester or a pair programmer

### Is there a free AI coding tool?

Yes. Codeium, Cody, Kite, and Continue.dev all offer free tiers, with Continue.dev and Cody supporting local, private runs

### Are AI coding tools safe for proprietary code?

Cloud tools may send context externally. For sensitive repos, use local options like Tabnine or Continue.dev

### Do they replace code review?

No. Tools like Codium AI assist review, but a human must still verify correctness and security

Fit depends on your starting material and your constraints, and no ranked list can answer that for you. Begin with a single task and one tool, and expand when the return is obvious.
